content: Below is a detailed explanation of the recommended medical interventions: 1. Fluid Administration in Adults: Administer 1 liter of intravenous (IV) fluids over 30 minutes or faster. Reassess the patient immediately after the fluid has been infused. Look for signs of dehydration and shock. If shock persists after the initial bolus, repeat the crystalloid fluid bolus. Severely ill adults with significant GI losses may require 3 to 6 liters of fluids daily. If severe dehydration is present, refer to Plan C for fluid requirements. Monitor the patient closely for signs of response to treatment and fluid overload. Continue fluid administration until hydration targets are achieved or signs of fluid overload are observed. Check respiratory rate before and after each bolus. Use a pulse oximeter, if available, to monitor heart rate and oxygen saturation. If the patient’s condition does not improve, consider adding vasopressors if operationally feasible. 2. Hydration Targets in Adults: Heart rate (HR) < 100 beats per minute. Urine output > 30 mL/hour. Additional markers of adequate perfusion include capillary refill time < 3 seconds, absence of skin mottling, palpable peripheral pulses, warm and dry extremities, and improved mental status. 3. Management of Severe Ebola Cases with Emergency Signs: Reassess the need for IV fluids every 8 hours. Reduce IV fluids to maintenance levels once the patient no longer shows signs of shock (e.g. If the patient is ambulatory and tolerating oral fluids, discontinue IV fluids. 4. Electrolyte and Glucose Management: Electrolyte abnormalities from GI losses can lead to life-threatening complications such as arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, or seizures. Use point-of-care testing to monitor and correct electrolyte imbalances. For hypokalemia, add 20 mEq of potassium chloride (KCl) to each liter of IV fluids. If testing is unavailable, empirically add 10 mEq KCl per liter in cases of significant vomiting or diarrhea. Provide oral rehydration salts (ORS) rather than plain water and consider oral potassium supplements (40 mEq/day) for patients who can tolerate oral intake. Note that Lactated Ringer’s solution contains only 4 mEq/L of potassium, while ORS contains 20 mEq/L. Encourage patients to sip ORS while receiving IV fluids. Correct hypomagnesemia, which is common in Ebola patients, as it aids in resolving hypokalemia. Use intravenous magnesium (2–4 g over 1 hour) instead of oral magnesium, which may worsen diarrhea. 5. Hypoglycemia Management: Hypoglycemia can result in seizures, coma, or death, particularly in critically ill adults, children, elderly patients, or those with severe malnutrition. Check glucose levels with a bedside glucometer and replenish as needed. Add ampoules of D50 (50% dextrose) to IV fluids to provide glucose. 6. Antibiotic Therapy for Patients with Large GI Losses: Consider empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone, for patients with significant abdominal symptoms or suspected secondary bacterial infections due to gut bacterial translocation. If GI complaints worsen or bloody diarrhea occurs in patients without confirmed Ebola, add metronidazole to cover anaerobic infections, including Clostridium difficile. For confirmed Ebola cases, discontinue antibiotics after 5 days if symptoms improve and there is no other indication to continue. 7. Septic Shock Management in Adolescents and Adults: Septic shock may coexist with hypovolemic shock in Ebola patients due to the virus or secondary infections. Clinical diagnosis of septic shock includes suspected infection, hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg), and one or more of the following: pulse > 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate > 24 breaths per minute, or abnormal temperature (< 36°C or > 38°C). Administer oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 90%. Begin IV fluids rapidly, starting with a 1,000 mL bolus of Lactated Ringer’s or normal saline, followed by 20 mL/kg/hour up to 60 mL/kg within the first 2 hours. If SBP remains < 90 mmHg after 2 hours, consider vasopressors (dopamine, norepinephrine, or epinephrine) if available and feasible for continuous monitoring. Administer empirical antibiotics within the first hour, such as ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily. If malaria is suspected, start IV artesunate. For confirmed Lassa fever or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), consider ribavirin. 8. Monitoring and Response: Monitor SBP, pulse, respiratory rate, SpO2, mental status, and JVP every 30 minutes until stable, then hourly. Check for signs of fluid overload, such as increased respiratory rate, elevated JVP, or crackles on auscultation. If fluid overload is suspected, slow the rate of fluid administration and consider starting vasopressors if the patient remains in shock. 9. Nutritional Support: Patients should continue eating and drinking ORS even while on IV fluids. Offer small, frequent meals and soft foods, which are often better tolerated. For patients unable to swallow safely, consider nasogastric feeding with semi-solid foods. Monitor for signs of malnutrition and provide appropriate nutritional support, such as F75 therapeutic milk for children. 10. Special Considerations for Children: Children with shock and severe dehydration, malnutrition, or anemia require tailored fluid resuscitation. Administer 10–20 mL/kg of IV fluids over 30–60 minutes, depending on the severity of their condition. For children with severe malnutrition, give 10–15 mL/kg of IV fluids over the first hour. If improvement occurs, switch to oral or nasogastric maintenance fluids. Reassess hydration status frequently and monitor for signs of fluid overload, cardiac failure, or neurological deterioration. If these occur, stop IV fluids immediately. 11. Blood Transfusion: For children with severe anemia (Hb < 5 g/dL), arrange for an urgent blood transfusion. Administer 10 mL/kg of whole blood over at least 3 hours. Reassess the child’s condition after the transfusion and monitor for any signs of deterioration. By following these detailed protocols, healthcare providers can effectively manage patients with severe dehydration, shock, or complications related to Ebola or other critical illnesses.
